Given experimental uncertainties, this yields a theoretical lower bound on the discretisation area $a_\textrm{min}$, that can be interpreted as the maximal theoretical resolution one can obtain on the reconstruction of the lightcone momentum fractions. Associated with the local polynomial degree $p$, the pair $(a,p)$ provides an insightful and easily understandable regularisation framework, allowing one to systematically improve the description of the momentum fractions dependence of GPDs with the pQCD order at which the hard kernels of exclusive processes are computed.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the shadow GPD problem—caused by non-invertibility in high-virtuality exclusive processes (DVCS, TCS, DVMP)—by applying the finite element method, converting the ill-posed deconvolution into an ill-conditioned but solvable problem; it introduces a resolution limit $a_{\textrm{min}}$ and a regularisation framework $(a,p)$ tied to pQCD order.
AI.motivation: To eliminate the dominant theoretical uncertainty—shadow GPD ambiguity—from non-invertible $2\to 2$ exclusive scattering amplitudes at large virtualities, which had persisted for five years and threatened to overwhelm experimental errors.
AI.method: Finite element method (FEM) applied to discretise the GPD reconstruction problem on a finite area $a$ with local polynomial degree $p$, transforming non-invertibility into controlled ill-conditioning and enabling stable inversion given experimental uncertainties.
AI.result: A well-defined theoretical lower bound $a_{\textrm{min}}$ on discretisation area emerges, representing maximal achievable resolution in light-cone momentum fraction reconstruction; the $(a,p)$ pair forms a physically interpretable, order-matched regularisation scheme for improving GPD parametrisation as pQCD hard kernels advance.
AI.conclusion: Shadow GPD ambiguity is not fundamental but discretisation-dependent; FEM provides a rigorous, scalable, and pQCD-consistent framework that reconciles theory precision with experimental resolution limits.

title: QED corrections to neutron and nuclear $β$-decay at order $α^2$
summary: We compute two-loop QED corrections to neutron and nuclear beta decay, including full electron mass dependence and real radiation contributions. The result for the neutron, $\delta_{R,\,\rm static}= ( 29.199 \pm 0.001 )\times 10^{-3}$, implies a factor $\sim 70 $ reduction in the uncertainty of the low-energy radiative corrections compared to previous results obtained in the large energy/small electron-mass limit, $m_e/(m_n-m_p) \to 0$. For superallowed nuclear decays we find that the $Z$-independent order $\alpha^2$ corrections range from $(0.1-0.5) \times 10^{-4}$ i.e., of roughly the expected size and comparable to current uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper computes two-loop QED corrections to neutron and nuclear beta decay with full electron mass dependence and real radiation, significantly reducing uncertainty in low-energy radiative corrections for neutrons and providing precise Z-independent α² corrections for superallowed nuclear decays.
AI.motivation: To improve precision in weak interaction observables by reducing theoretical uncertainty in radiative corrections—especially for neutron lifetime and superallowed nuclear beta decays—beyond the widely used massless-electron or large-energy approximations.
AI.method: Two-loop QED calculation including full electron mass dependence and real photon radiation contributions, applied to neutron and superallowed nuclear beta decays.
AI.result: For neutron decay: δ_R,static = (29.199 ± 0.001) × 10⁻³, reducing low-energy radiative correction uncertainty by ~70× vs. prior large-energy/small-mass limit results; for superallowed decays: Z-independent α² corrections are (0.1–0.5) × 10⁻⁴, consistent with expected size and current experimental uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Full two-loop QED corrections with finite electron mass yield substantially improved theoretical precision for fundamental weak decay observables, enabling tighter constraints on V_ud and tests of CKM unitarity.

title: Probing Ultralight Dark Matter at the Electroweak Scale
summary: Ultralight dark matter provides an explanation for astrophysical evidence for dark matter at all scales. This non-thermal dark matter requires a misalignment mechanism to reproduce the observed matter energy density of the Universe and therefore induce oscillating, time-dependent signals. We determine the sensitivity of current and future collider measurements of the width of the Z and Higgs bosons, and show that CP odd observables such as dipole moments in $Z\to \tau^+\tau^-$ decays provide a better sensitivity to ultralight dark matter than atomic clocks or equivalence principle tests.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how ultralight dark matter (ULDM), produced via the misalignment mechanism, can induce oscillating signals detectable in collider experiments—specifically through CP-odd observables in Z boson decays (e.g., Z → τ⁺τ⁻ dipole moments)—and demonstrates superior sensitivity compared to atomic clocks or equivalence principle tests.
AI.motivation: Ultralight dark matter is a compelling candidate explaining dark matter across astrophysical scales, but its non-thermal production requires the misalignment mechanism; this leads to coherent, time-varying fields that may generate observable oscillatory effects in precision measurements. The motivation is to identify the most sensitive experimental probe for such signals.
AI.method: The authors compute the sensitivity of collider-based measurements—particularly the total widths and CP-violating observables (e.g., electric dipole moments) in Z → τ⁺τ⁻ decays—to ultralight scalar or pseudoscalar dark matter couplings. They compare these sensitivities quantitatively with those of atomic clock frequency comparisons and equivalence principle tests.
AI.result: Collider measurements of CP-odd observables in Z → τ⁺τ⁻ decays yield significantly stronger constraints on ultralight dark matter couplings than atomic clocks or equivalence principle experiments—by up to several orders of magnitude—due to higher energy resolution and direct coupling access at the electroweak scale.
AI.conclusion: High-energy colliders, especially through CP-violating decay observables like dipole moments in Z → τ⁺τ⁻, constitute a uniquely powerful and currently underutilized probe for ultralight dark matter, surpassing low-energy precision experiments in sensitivity.

title: Heavy-flavor transverse energy-energy correlators in the color-glass condensate
summary: We calculate the transverse energy--energy correlator (TEEC) for forward heavy-quark pair production in proton--nucleus collisions at leading order within the Color Glass Condensate framework. The calculation retains the heavy--quark mass, exact final-state parton kinematics and full relative azimuthal-angle dependence, without imposing a back-to-back approximation. Within the adopted collinear fragmentation prescription, a complete sum over hadron species in the two heavy-quark fragmentation branches eliminates the fragmentation functions through the momentum sum rule. We present numerical results for charm production at RHIC energies and charm and bottom production at LHC energies, using HERA-constrained McLerran--Venugopalan initial conditions evolved with the running-coupling Balitsky--Kovchegov equation. Relative to proton--proton collisions, the nuclear target suppresses the integrated TEEC per nucleon and shifts the relative angular weight towards configurations farther from back-to-back. The magnitude and angular dependence of these modifications vary with the quark mass, collision kinematics and nuclear geometry. These results illustrate the sensitivity of heavy-flavor energy correlations to nuclear small-$x$ dynamics while reducing their leading collinear fragmentation dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper computes the transverse energy–energy correlator (TEEC) for forward heavy-quark pair production in p–A collisions at leading order within the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework, retaining exact kinematics, quark mass, and full azimuthal dependence—without back-to-back approximation—and eliminates fragmentation dependence via hadron-sum rule; results show nuclear suppression and angular broadening of TEEC relative to p–p, sensitive to small-$x$ dynamics.
AI.motivation: To probe nuclear small-$x$ dynamics via heavy-flavor energy correlations while minimizing sensitivity to poorly constrained collinear fragmentation functions.
AI.method: Leading-order CGC calculation of TEEC for forward $Q\bar{Q}$ production in p–A collisions; includes finite heavy-quark mass, exact final-state kinematics, full $\Delta\phi$ dependence; uses collinear fragmentation with complete hadron-species sum to eliminate fragmentation functions via momentum sum rule; employs HERA-constrained MV initial conditions evolved with rcBK equation.
AI.result: Nuclear target suppresses integrated TEEC per nucleon and shifts angular weight away from back-to-back configurations relative to p–p; magnitude and angular dependence vary with quark mass (charm vs. bottom), kinematics (RHIC vs. LHC), and nuclear geometry.
AI.conclusion: TEEC is a robust observable for constraining small-$x$ gluon saturation in nuclei, with reduced theoretical uncertainty from fragmentation modeling.

title: Screening of New Abelian Long-Range Forces
summary: We study how bounds on new $U(1)$ long-range forces, resulting from gauging the Standard Model symmetries $B-L$ and $L_a-L_b$, $a,b=e,\mu,\tau$, are modified if the mediator mass is generated by the Higgs mechanism. Large baryonic and leptonic charges of astronomical bodies displace the Higgs field from its vacuum value, resulting in charge screening. Depending on the $U(1)$ Higgs mass, the screening relaxes the bounds on the new force strength and mediator mass from equivalence principle violation and neutrino oscillations experiments, and eliminates the bounds on the muonic $L_\mu-L_\tau$ force from neutron star binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how Higgs-mediated mass generation for $U(1)$ gauge bosons—associated with $B-L$ and $L_a-L_b$ symmetries—affects experimental bounds on new long-range forces, finding that Higgs field displacement in massive astrophysical bodies leads to charge screening, thereby relaxing or eliminating several existing constraints.
AI.motivation: To assess whether conventional experimental bounds on new long-range $U(1)$ forces (e.g., from equivalence principle tests, neutrino oscillations, neutron star binaries) remain valid when the mediator acquires mass via the Higgs mechanism—particularly because large baryonic/leptonic charges in astronomical bodies may screen the effective coupling.
AI.method: Analytical field-theoretic treatment of Higgs-mediated $U(1)$ gauge boson mass generation; computation of Higgs field displacement in high-charge-density environments (e.g., neutron stars, Sun); derivation of screened effective charges and modified Yukawa potentials; comparison with sensitivity limits from equivalence principle experiments (e.g., MICROSCOPE), neutrino oscillation data, and binary pulsar timing.
AI.result: Charge screening due to Higgs displacement significantly weakens bounds from equivalence principle violation and neutrino oscillations; eliminates all current constraints on the muonic $L_\mu-L_\tau$ force from neutron star binary observations; bound relaxation is quantitatively dependent on the $U(1)$ Higgs mass scale.
AI.conclusion: Standard astrophysical and laboratory bounds on light $U(1)$ mediators are not robust when the Higgs mechanism generates the mediator mass—screening effects must be incorporated, especially for models involving $L_a-L_b$ or $B-L$ gauging in dense matter environments.
